conventional_description:
Bile duct stones (choledocholithiasis) occur when hardened deposits of digestive fluid form in the common bile duct, the tube that carries bile from the liver and gallbladder to the small intestine. They can cause sudden, severe pain in the upper right abdomen, jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes), dark urine, nausea, and fever.
Diagnosis is typically made through imaging such as ultrasound, CT scan, or MRCP (magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography). Left untreated, they can lead to serious infections like cholangitis or pancreatitis.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment often involves endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) to remove stones from the duct, sometimes with sphincterotomy. In more complex cases, surgery may be needed to remove the gallbladder (cholecystectomy) or to drain the duct. Antibiotics are used if infection is present. For patients who are not candidates for procedures, medications to dissolve stones (like ursodeoxycholic acid) may be tried, though they are less effective for duct stones than for gallbladder stones.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, bile duct stones are not simply a mechanical blockage - they are a sign that the body's flow has stalled. The Liver and Gallbladder are paired organs responsible for the smooth movement of Qi and the secretion of bile. When this flow is disrupted by emotional stress, dietary excess, or constitutional weakness, bile becomes stagnant, thickens, and eventually hardens into stones.
The specific disruption determines the pattern. Emotional frustration and anger cause Liver Qi Stagnation, where energy gets stuck and bile backs up, leading to distending pain that worsens with stress. Overindulgence in greasy, spicy, or rich foods creates Damp-Heat, a turbid, overheated condition that condenses bile into sludge and stones, often with fever and jaundice. Long-standing illness or overwork can deplete Liver Yin, leaving bile without the cooling, moistening fluids it needs to stay thin, resulting in a dull, chronic ache with dry mouth and night sweats.
In more severe cases, prolonged obstruction leads to Blood Stagnation, with fixed, knifelike pain, or even Toxic-Heat, a dangerous systemic infection marked by high fever and deep jaundice. Each of these five patterns requires a fundamentally different treatment strategy - which is why TCM does not have a single 'stone-dissolving' remedy, but instead tailors herbs and acupuncture to the exact imbalance at play.
classical_quote: 「太阳病，过经十余日，反二三下之，后四五日，柴胡证仍在者，先与小柴胡。呕不止，心下急，郁郁微烦者，为未解也，与大柴胡汤下之则愈。」
classical_translation: "In a combined Shaoyang and Yangming disease with persistent vomiting, epigastric fullness, and slight irritability, use Da Chai Hu Tang to purge and resolve. This describes the classic presentation of bile duct obstruction with Damp-Heat, where harmonizing Shaoyang and clearing interior heat restores bile flow."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner first listens carefully to how the pain actually feels. Is it a dull ache, a sharp stab, or a distending pressure? They also note whether fever, jaundice, or emotional upset accompany the pain. These details, together with tongue and pulse signs, quickly narrow down which of the five main patterns is driving the stones.
If the pain is severe, constant, and accompanied by a heavy sensation, yellowing of the skin, dark urine, and a bitter taste in the mouth, Liver and Gallbladder Damp-Heat is likely. The tongue is red with a thick greasy yellow coating, and the pulse feels slippery and rapid. This pattern often flares after heavy, fatty meals.
When the discomfort is a wandering, distending ache that moves around the ribs and clearly worsens with stress or frustration, Liver Qi Stagnation is the main picture. There is usually no fever or jaundice. The tongue appears pale or slightly red with a thin white coating, and the pulse has a tight, wiry quality that reflects blocked energy.
A dull, lingering ache in the right ribs with a sensation of heat, dry mouth, and night sweats points to Liver Yin Deficiency. This pattern often appears in chronic cases or during recovery. The tongue is red with little or no coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid, showing that the body’s cooling, moistening resources have been depleted over time.
A sharp, fixed pain that feels like a knife in one spot, with a tongue that looks dark purple or shows tiny purple spots, indicates Blood Stagnation. The pulse feels wiry and choppy, as if it stumbles. This arises when a stone has caused long‑standing local obstruction and tissue damage, and it may overlap with other patterns that have been present for a while.
The most dangerous pattern, Toxic-Heat, brings high fever, intense unrelenting pain, and deep jaundice. The tongue is deep red, and the pulse is flooding and rapid. This is a medical emergency signaling severe infection, and it requires immediate hospital care rather than self‑assessment or home remedies.

patterns.symptoms: ["Severe right upper abdominal pain", "Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice)", "Dark scanty urine", "Bitter taste in the mouth", "Fever and chills", "Thick, yellow, greasy tongue coating"]
patterns.worse_with: Fatty, greasy, or fried foods, Alcohol, Emotional stress, anger, or frustration, Overeating or heavy meals
patterns.better_with: Light, low-fat meals, Staying well hydrated, Gentle exercise or movement, Warm compress on abdomen or rib area
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Liver's smooth flow of Qi is disrupted-often by rich food, alcohol, or emotional stress-it creates a stagnant, overheated environment. Dampness and Heat then accumulate in the Gallbladder, much like mud thickening in a slow-moving stream. Over time, this turbid Damp-Heat condenses the bile, forming stones that block the ducts and cause sudden, intense pain, jaundice, and nausea.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, especially on the sides, with a thick yellow greasy coating. Pulse: wiry, slippery, and rapid (弦滑数).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Fatty and greasy foods directly create more Dampness and Heat, thickening the bile and triggering painful spasms. Alcohol is purely heating and dampening, worsening the internal environment. Emotional stress, especially anger and frustration, causes Liver Qi to stagnate, which is the root of this pattern. Gentle movement and warmth help Qi flow smoothly, while light, hydrating foods clear Heat and reduce the burden on the Liver and Gallbladder.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, and spicy foods, as well as alcohol-these directly feed Damp-Heat. Eat small, light meals with plenty of steamed vegetables and moderate whole grains. Gentle daily movement like walking helps Qi circulate, and managing stress prevents Liver Qi stagnation that fuels this pattern.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body, including the secretion of bile. When emotional stress, frustration, or anger build up, the Liver Qi becomes stuck and cannot move freely. This stagnation causes bile to slow down and thicken, gradually forming stones in the ducts. The hallmark is a distending, moving pain under the right ribs that comes and goes with your mood.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or light red body, red or slightly purple on the sides, thin white coating. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), taut like a guitar string.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress is the direct trigger for Liver Qi stagnation, which causes bile to become sluggish and form stones. Fatty and greasy foods overload the Liver and Gallbladder, making the stagnation worse. Gentle movement and relaxation help unblock stuck Qi, allowing bile to flow freely again. Warmth relaxes the Liver channel and eases the spasm-like distension. Eating small, regular meals prevents bile from sitting too long and thickening.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep meals small, light, and regular-avoid skipping breakfast, which can concentrate bile. Cut back on fatty, fried, and greasy foods that burden the Liver. Gentle daily exercise like walking or tai chi is one of the best ways to unstick Liver Qi. Make time for stress relief: deep breathing, journaling, or talking things out can make a big difference.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Liver Yin is depleted, the Liver and Gallbladder lose the cooling, moistening fluids that keep bile thin and free-flowing. Bile becomes thick and stagnant, gradually forming stones. The empty heat that arises from Yin deficiency adds a low-grade burning quality to the pain, while the lack of nourishment makes the hypochondrium ache dully rather than sharply.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, dry body with red sides and little or no coating. Pulse: wiry, fine, and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spicy, fried, and greasy foods, as well as alcohol, generate heat and consume Yin fluids, making bile thicker and the empty heat stronger. Late nights and overwork directly drain the body's Yin reserves. Stress and frustration stir Liver Yang, which further exhausts Yin. In contrast, moistening foods and adequate rest nourish Yin and cool empty heat, while gentle movement keeps Qi flowing without creating stagnation or overheating.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, fried, and greasy foods, as well as alcohol and coffee-they deplete Yin and generate heat. Eat moistening, cooling foods like pear, lily bulb, black sesame, goji berries, tofu, and millet. Go to bed early and avoid late-night screen time; Yin is replenished during sleep. Gentle exercise like tai chi or walking supports Qi flow without overheating the body.

patterns.why_this_happens:
When bile duct stones persist for a long time, the smooth flow of Qi and Blood through the Liver and Gallbladder channels becomes severely obstructed. The stagnant Qi eventually congeals into static Blood, which lodges in the bile ducts. This creates a fixed, stabbing pain that feels like a knife twisting in one spot, because the stuck Blood presses on the surrounding tissues.
Unlike the distending ache of Qi stagnation or the burning discomfort of Damp-Heat, this pain is piercing, worse at night (when Blood circulation naturally slows), and aggravated by any pressure on the area.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple or dusky body, possible stasis spots, distended dark sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩 sè) and wiry (弦 xián).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood stasis arises when Qi and Blood stop flowing freely. Gentle movement and warmth encourage circulation, while prolonged inactivity and cold congeal Blood further. Stress and anger knot the Liver Qi, which is the root of this stasis, so calming the mind helps unlock the flow. Fatty foods overwhelm the Liver and Gallbladder, creating more stagnation and pain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat lightly, avoiding greasy, fried, and heavy foods that burden the Liver and Gallbladder. Gentle daily walks keep Qi and Blood moving, preventing further stagnation. Manage emotional stress with deep breathing or tai chi, as anger and frustration can worsen Liver Qi stagnation and deepen blood stasis.

patterns.why_this_happens: When damp-heat and fire toxin accumulate intensely in the liver and gallbladder, they can boil over into a dangerous systemic heat crisis. This extreme heat damages the bile ducts, causing severe swelling, pus formation, and blockage. The result is a sudden high fever, intense constant pain, and deep jaundice - a medical emergency that requires immediate care.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: deep red with prickly thorns, dry yellow or gray-black coating. Pulse: flooding (hong) and rapid (shu), forceful.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work:
Toxic-Heat is an extreme form of internal Fire and damp-heat, so anything that adds heat or stagnation makes it worse. Spicy and greasy foods generate more damp-heat and fire toxin, while emotional stress and anger stir up liver fire, feeding the crisis. Physical exertion fans the internal flame and can spread the toxin.

Cooling measures - a quiet environment, rest, and cold compresses - help settle the raging heat. Warm water gently supports fluid balance without shocking the system. In this dangerous stage, the goal is to drain the fire toxin and restore bile flow as quickly as possible, which is why purging and clearing formulas are used.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: This is an acute, serious stage. Fasting or a liquid-only diet may be recommended under medical supervision. Avoid all greasy, fried, spicy, and rich foods, as well as alcohol. Sip warm water or light herbal teas like chrysanthemum to help cool the body. Absolute rest is essential; any physical exertion can worsen the condition.

faqs.question: Can TCM dissolve bile duct stones?
faqs.answer: Yes, but the approach depends on your pattern. Herbal formulas are designed to change the internal environment that allowed stones to form - by clearing damp-heat, moving stagnant qi, or nourishing yin - so that stones can gradually soften and pass or dissolve. This is not an overnight process; it typically takes weeks to months. In acute, large, or obstructing stones, conventional removal may still be necessary, and TCM can be used alongside to speed recovery and prevent recurrence.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture effective for bile duct stone pain?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture can be very helpful for managing the pain and discomfort of bile duct stones, especially during acute episodes. Points like Yanglingquan (GB-34) and Danshu (BL-19) help relax the bile duct, relieve spasms, and promote bile flow. It is often used in combination with herbal therapy for best results.

faqs.question: Can I combine TCM with ERCP or surgery?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. TCM can be used before a procedure to reduce inflammation and optimize your overall health, and after a procedure to support healing, prevent infection, and reduce the risk of stone recurrence. Always inform your gastroenterologist and TCM practitioner about all treatments you are receiving so they can coordinate your care safely.

faqs.question: What diet should I follow while undergoing TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: In general, avoid greasy, fried, and spicy foods, alcohol, and excessive dairy, as these create dampness and heat - the very conditions that promote stone formation. Favour light, cooked meals with plenty of vegetables, whole grains, and moderate lean protein. Eating smaller, more frequent meals and never skipping breakfast helps keep bile flowing.

faqs.question: How do I know which TCM pattern I have?
faqs.answer: A qualified TCM practitioner will determine your pattern through a detailed consultation that includes listening to your symptoms, examining your tongue, and feeling your pulse. For example, a red tongue with a thick yellow coating and a rapid, slippery pulse suggests Damp-Heat, while a pale tongue with a thin white coating and a wiry pulse points to Liver Qi Stagnation. Self-assessment quizzes can give you a general idea, but professional diagnosis is essential before starting treatment.

faqs.question: Are there any risks with herbal medicine for bile duct stones?
faqs.answer: When prescribed by a trained practitioner, TCM herbs are generally safe. However, some herbs that move blood or clear heat can interact with medications like anticoagulants. Always provide a full list of your medications and supplements to your TCM practitioner. In rare cases, strong stone-dissolving herbs can cause temporary loose stools or mild abdominal cramping, which usually subside as your body adjusts.

faqs.question: Will the stones come back after TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to correct the underlying imbalance that caused the stones, so recurrence rates are generally lower than with procedures that only remove the stones. However, if you return to dietary and lifestyle habits that created the imbalance, stones can form again. Your practitioner will guide you on long-term dietary and lifestyle adjustments to maintain a healthy bile flow.

research.title: Consensus Opinion on Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine for Diagnosis and Treatment of Cholelithiasis (2017)
research.description: This national consensus guideline outlines TCM syndrome differentiation for gallstones, including bile duct stones, and recommends herbal formulas such as Da Chai Hu Tang for Liver and Gallbladder Damp-Heat and Chai Hu Shu Gan San for Liver Qi Stagnation. It integrates modern diagnostic criteria with TCM treatment protocols.
research.periodical: Chinese Association of Integrative Medicine, Digestive Disease Committee. Consensus Opinion on Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine for Diagnosis and Treatment of Cholelithiasis (2017). Chinese Journal of Integrated Traditional and Western Medicine on Digestion, 2018.

research.title: Expert Consensus on Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine Diagnosis and Treatment of Gallstones (2025)
research.description: An updated expert consensus providing detailed TCM pattern differentiation, treatment principles, and integrated management strategies for gallstones and bile duct stones, emphasizing the role of acupuncture and herbal medicine alongside conventional care.
research.periodical: Chinese Association of Integrative Medicine. Expert Consensus on Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine Diagnosis and Treatment of Gallstones (2025). Journal of Clinical Hepatology, 2025.

research.title: Da-Chai-Hu-Tang Protects From Acute Intrahepatic Cholestasis by Inhibiting Hepatic Inflammation and Bile Accumulation via Activation of PPARα
research.description: This mechanistic study demonstrates that Da Chai Hu Tang, a classic formula for Damp-Heat in the Liver and Gallbladder, reduces bile acid accumulation and hepatic inflammation in a rat model of cholestasis. The findings support its traditional use in bile duct obstruction and stone-related jaundice.
research.periodical: Wang X, et al. Da-Chai-Hu-Tang Protects From Acute Intrahepatic Cholestasis by Inhibiting Hepatic Inflammation and Bile Accumulation via Activation of PPARα. Front Pharmacol. 2022;13:896532.

research.title: Acupuncture Treatment of a Case of Gallstones
research.description: A case report of a 45-year-old female with gallstones and bile duct stones treated with acupuncture at points including Yanglingquan (GB-34), Danshu (BL-19), and Qimen (LR-14). After 12 sessions, ultrasound showed a reduction in stone size and complete resolution of pain, suggesting acupuncture can promote bile flow and stone passage.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, et al. Acupuncture Treatment of a Case of Gallstones. Traditional Chinese Medicine. 2024;13(7):1372-1377.
